archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (broken offense)
archetype.definition: A 1-9 team whose point differential says it should have about four wins, but whose offense is bad enough that the gap only lifts it from historically bad to merely poor.

report.headline: Bad luck explains part of 1-9; a broken offense explains the rest.
report.take:
The Chargers arrived in 2026 off back-to-back 11-win seasons built on defense. In 2024 they allowed the fewest points in the league, and in 2025 they ranked sixth in defensive EPA. The offense was already sliding last year: 23rd in EPA, carried by a 0.75 one-score win rate. This season the defense came back to the pack, the offense fell off the floor, and the close-game luck flipped. That is how a team with Jim Harbaugh and a healthy Justin Herbert for ten straight starts ends up 1-9.

The offense is the story. It ranks last in EPA per play and last in pass rate over expected at -10.3. Harbaugh keeps leaning on the run even though the run game is the league's worst by run EPA (-0.267), and the line ranks 23rd in both stuff rate and yards before contact. Throwing hasn't been a refuge either. The line ranks 31st in sack rate, Herbert has taken 39 sacks, and the line leads the league in penalties per game. Add 19 turnovers and you get 16.8 points a game, with most drives dying behind the chains or on a giveaway.

The numbers hide two things. First, this isn't a one-win team on talent. The -98 differential implies 4.3 wins, and Wins Over Expected of -3.25 ranks dead last. Several losses came by one score and none of those swung their way. This franchise has been here before: in 2019 and 2023 it posted nearly identical luck numbers. Second, the defense is ordinary rather than bad. It ranks 15th in EPA allowed, seventh on third down and ninth in takeaways. Points allowed run worse than that because turnovers keep handing opponents short fields. Its real holes are a thin pass rush (24th in pressure rate) and getting beaten deep.

Where it goes from here depends on whether the last two weeks were real. Against Baltimore and the Jets the Chargers had no turnovers. The Jets game produced their only positive passing and rushing EPA in the same game. Herbert then left in the concussion protocol. With him and better ball security, this is a team that steals two or three more games. Without him, the schedule's back half (San Francisco, Kansas City, Denver) offers little mercy.

strengths.title: Defense that gets off the field
strengths.body: The unit has slipped from elite to average but still wins the money downs. It ranks seventh in third-down rate allowed and ninth in takeaways. Its tackling is sound, with the ninth-lowest missed-tackle rate, which keeps short completions short. That holds up because it rests on structure, not a pass rush that has dried up.

strengths.title: Containing the top receiver
strengths.body: Opposing WR1s have scored 3.4 PPR points a game under their usual output, sixth-best in the league. The TE1 is held under as well. Secondary receivers do more damage, which suggests coverage tilted toward the main threat. With Tarheeb Still out, that tilt gets harder to hold.

strengths.title: A late offensive pulse
strengths.body: After bottoming out in Weeks 6 and 8, the offense played two clean games: no turnovers against Baltimore or the Jets. Against New York it posted its best passing and rushing EPA of the season in the same game. Two games is a thin sample, but ball security is the most fixable thing on this roster.

concerns.title: Protection is a full-blown crisis
concerns.body: Herbert has been sacked 39 times. The line ranks 31st in both sack rate and QB hit rate allowed, and it leads the league in line penalties per game. Even the good Jets game included six sacks, and Houston got eight. This is structural: it has persisted through every game. Now it comes with a concussed quarterback, which raises the stakes.

concerns.title: Run-first with the worst run game
concerns.body: No team passes less than expected than the Chargers. Yet their run EPA is the league's worst and their run success rate ranks 27th. Shielding a bad pass-protecting line explains the choice, but it caps the offense: early-down runs that go nowhere create the long-yardage downs where the line breaks down. That is a coaching identity choice, and nothing suggests it changes this year.

concerns.title: Giveaways and flags bleed points
concerns.body: Nineteen turnovers against 14 takeaways leave them at -5, and the 8.3 penalties a game rank 29th. The giveaways are a big reason an average defense allows 26.6 points a game. Turnover rates swing a lot from year to year, so some improvement is likely. The penalties look more like a habit.

trend.note: Passing EPA sank steadily to season lows in Weeks 6 and 8, then climbed in each of the last three games, finishing positive against the Jets. The protection numbers have not followed, and Herbert's concussion could stall the climb.

nextGame.headline: Two backup-QB scares meet in a 35.5-total coin flip
nextGame.body:
New England is a 5-5 team that has been average on both sides of the ball, but the matchup shape suits the Chargers if Herbert plays. The Patriots' pass defense ranks 23rd in EPA allowed and 29th in explosive pass rate. Opposing WR1s and WR2s have feasted on them, ranking 32nd and 31st in EPA per target. Their run defense is far sturdier, 11th in rush EPA allowed. That is exactly where Harbaugh likes to live, so the plan has to bend toward Tre Harris and Quentin Johnston. The Patriots also give the ball away a lot, ranking 31st in turnover differential per game. The danger is their pass rush, eighth in sack rate, against a line that ranks 31st in sack rate allowed.

Availability drives the line. Herbert is questionable in the concussion protocol, with DJ Uiagalelei behind him. Cornerback Tarheeb Still and linebacker Daiyan Henley are out, which thins the back seven. New England is without Drake Maye, out with a fractured fibula, after he started every game this year. A.J. Brown is doubtful, while Romeo Doubs could return from IR. The Patriots are also missing cornerback Carlton Davis and center Ben Brown. The Book has the Chargers at -1.5 with a 35.5 total, a pick'em that expects both offenses to struggle.

waysToWin.title: Throw at New England's leaky corners
waysToWin.body: The Patriots allow big plays through the air and get torched by top receivers, and Carlton Davis is out. A healthy Herbert taking early-down shots to Harris and Johnston, instead of running into a solid run defense, is the clearest edge on the board.

waysToWin.title: Feast on a backup quarterback
waysToWin.body: New England's offense was built around Maye, and his replacement has no starts this year. The Patriots already turn it over at one of the league's worst rates. A Chargers defense that ranks seventh on third down and ninth in takeaways can win this game outright if it forces short fields.

waysToWin.title: Repeat two clean weeks
waysToWin.body: In a game with a 35.5 total, possessions are precious. Zero turnovers in each of the last two games is the formula that produced the one win and a near-miss.

waysToLose.title: The pass rush swallows the pocket
waysToLose.body: New England ranks eighth in both sacks and sack rate. The Chargers have allowed six or more sacks twice in their last three games. Drive-killing sacks against a run defense that won't give up the ground game leave this offense in the low teens.

waysToLose.title: Herbert sits, the offense stalls
waysToLose.body: If Herbert doesn't clear the protocol, Uiagalelei takes over an offense already last in EPA, behind a line that can't protect. With no passing threat, New England can crowd the run, and its run defense is the strength of its unit.

waysToLose.title: A thinned secondary gets beaten deep
waysToLose.body: With Still and Henley out, the Chargers' deep defense, already 29th in EPA on deep throws, gets thinner. Even a backup quarterback can flip a low-scoring game with one shot over the top, especially if Doubs is back.

nextGame.watch: Whether Herbert clears the concussion protocol, and if he does, whether Harbaugh actually lets him throw at New England's vulnerable corners rather than running into their best unit.

restOfSeason.body:
Some regression toward the point differential is coming. A team that has played to roughly four wins' worth of football should not keep losing every close game, and the turnover rate should ease. The two clean games suggest ball security can improve. The protection problems and the run game look structural, and they won't go away in seven weeks. The defense is no longer the top-10 unit of the last two years. It should keep games close but can't win them alone.

The schedule splits cleanly. New England, Tampa Bay (a poor offense but a top-3 defense), Las Vegas and Miami are winnable. San Francisco, Kansas City and Denver look like losses. A healthy Herbert probably means two or three more wins. Any extended absence pushes that toward one, and with it a top draft slot.
swingFactors: Secondary health with Still and Henley out

confidence.note: Ten games is a solid read on the offense, but Herbert's concussion and the injured secondary cloud the near term.
